analysis.one_liner: Requires car and tire makers to quickly report safety defects and raises penalties for hiding them.
analysis.headline: Within a month of introduction it passed the House by voice vote and the Senate by unanimous consent, and was signed into law as Public Law 106-414 on November 1, 2000.
analysis.plain_summary: This law, written amid a major tire-safety scandal, forces auto and tire manufacturers to tell federal safety regulators within five working days when they recall a vehicle or part overseas that is also sold in the United States, and to hand over data on deaths, injuries, and warranty claims tied to possible defects. It extends the period during which manufacturers must fix recalled defects for free, requires reimbursing owners who already paid for a recall repair, raises civil penalties to as much as $15 million per related series of violations, and creates prison terms of up to 15 years for willfully misleading regulators about defects that caused death or serious injury. It also orders better tire standards and labeling, tire-pressure warning systems in new vehicles, rollover crash testing, and stronger child car seat safety rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, passengers, and families. Regulators get early warning of defects from the manufacturers' own records, so recalls can start sooner. Owners keep free recall repairs for 10 years on vehicles and 5 years on tires (up from 8 and 3), and get reimbursed if they paid out of pocket for a repair before the recall was announced. New vehicles must warn drivers when a tire is badly underinflated, tires must meet updated endurance standards, rollover test results must be published for shoppers, and child car seats face tougher testing and a public safety-ratings program.

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to report within 5 working days any decision — theirs or a foreign government's — to recall a vehicle or equipment identical or substantially similar to a product sold in the United States, so defects found abroad trigger scrutiny here too.

Orders a rulemaking forcing manufacturers to periodically report injury and death claims, warranty and property-damage data, and information on recalls and customer-satisfaction campaigns, both domestic and foreign.

Extends no-charge recall remedies from 8 to 10 calendar years for vehicles and from 3 to 5 years for tires, and requires manufacturers to include a plan to reimburse owners who paid for a recall remedy before the official defect notification.

Raises civil penalties to $5,000 per violation with a $15 million cap per related series of violations (and $5,000 per day for reporting violations), and adds criminal penalties of up to 15 years for willfully misleading the Secretary about defects that caused death or serious bodily injury.

Requires a tire-pressure warning system in new vehicles, an update of tire endurance standards and labeling, a dynamic rollover test with public results for consumer information, a ban on reselling replaced defective tires, and a rulemaking to improve child restraint safety with a public child-seat safety rating program.

analysis.who_pays: Motor vehicle, tire, and child-seat manufacturers, plus their dealers. They must build systems to collect and report defect and claims data, honor free recall remedies for longer, reimburse owners who pre-paid for repairs, absorb civil penalties of up to $15 million per related series of violations, and face criminal exposure for willfully misleading regulators about deadly defects.

drawbacks.text: The law tells the Secretary not to impose early-warning reporting requirements that are 'unduly burdensome' to manufacturers, weighing their cost of compliance — an industry-protective limit written into the core of the reporting rule.

Data collected under the early-warning rule generally may not be publicly disclosed unless the Secretary determines disclosure will help carry out the defect-investigation provisions, limiting public visibility into what manufacturers report.

The criminal penalty carries a safe harbor: no prosecution if the violator did not know the failure would cause death or serious injury and corrects the reporting within a reasonable time — and the criminal provision does not take effect until the Secretary writes rules defining that reasonable time.

The regime depends on manufacturers policing themselves by reporting from their own records, and Congress ordered only a study — not a mandate — on whether insurers' auto-accident claims data could be used for defect detection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real: manufacturers must build reporting systems, honor longer free-repair windows, and accept up to $15 million in penalties per related series of violations and criminal exposure for concealment. But the whole point of the bill is that this information existed inside companies and never reached regulators, while defective tires and vehicles were on American roads. The design leans on companies to report against their own interest, with limits on public disclosure and a bar on unduly burdensome requirements, so its real-world strength depends on regulators writing and enforcing a tough reporting rule — but on paper the public-safety gains clearly outweigh the compliance costs.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote under a fast-track procedure on October 10–11, 2000, the Senate passed it without amendment by unanimous consent the next day, and the President signed it on November 1, 2000.

narrative.text: Introduced September 13, 2000, it moved through committee in under a month: a subcommittee forwarded it 23-0 on September 27, and the full Commerce Committee reported it as amended by a 42-0 vote on October 5.
The House passed it as amended by voice vote under suspension of the rules — a fast-track procedure with limited debate — on October 10-11, 2000.
The Senate passed it the same month without amendment by unanimous consent, and the President signed it on November 1, 2000, making it Public Law 106-414.
The law repealed a defect-reporting provision Congress had added to the FY2001 transportation appropriations act and replaced it with this fuller framework.
It authorized $9.1 million for fiscal year 2001 to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to carry out the act.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill became law, drivers and families gained faster government detection of safety defects, longer free-remedy windows, reimbursement for pre-recall repairs, and stronger tire and child-seat standards. Manufacturers took on reporting duties and penalty exposure rather than getting a weaker version, as the law also replaced an earlier, narrower appropriations-act provision with the fuller framework.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drivers and families, through faster defect detection

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no opposition anywhere: the subcommittee forwarded the bill 23-0, the full committee reported it 42-0, the House passed it by voice vote, the Senate by unanimous consent, and its 41 cosponsors split 18 Republicans and 23 Democrats.

industries.note: The bill requires them to report foreign recalls within 5 working days, turn over warranty and death-and-injury claim data, honor free recall remedies for longer (10 years for vehicles, 5 for tires), reimburse owners who paid for pre-recall repairs, and face civil penalties up to $15 million per related series of violations and up to 15 years in prison for willfully misleading regulators about deadly defects. Their compliance costs and penalty exposure are the price of regulators learning about dangerous defects sooner.

The law orders a rulemaking on tougher child-seat testing, including side-impact crash tests and dummies representing more child sizes, plus a public safety-ratings program and at least $750,000 a year for crash testing. Their redesign and testing costs correspond to better-protected children.

The law bars selling or leasing replaced defective tires for installation on vehicles unless the defect is fixed first, and requires manufacturers' remedy plans to prevent resold recalled tires and limit their disposal in landfills. Profit from reselling known-defective tires came at the expense of the drivers who bought them.
